source.work: pstack principles (boundary, domain, reader load, idempotency, legacy deletion, proof)
source.paraphrase: Guards sit at the system boundary. Inside that boundary the code trusts its types and keeps the business rules free of framework adapters.

invariants.why: A validator in the domain makes the model depend on a parsing library and invites business rules to re-parse data they should already trust.
invariants.fixHint: Parse the request in the adapter, then call the domain with the type the parser returned.
invariants.avoid: A subpath such as zod/v4 is the same package. A relative barrel that re-exports the validator is a hole: the domain import no longer names the package.

source.work: pstack principles (boundary, domain, reader load, idempotency, legacy deletion, proof)
source.paraphrase: Refuse to lie to the checker. External data is parsed at the boundary so the domain never asserts a type it did not construct.

invariants.why: An assertion tells the checker to trust the author. In the domain that lie becomes a business rule that was never parsed.
invariants.fixHint: Parse untrusted input in the adapter. Inside the domain, narrow with a guard that returns the domain type.
invariants.avoid: `as const` is a value narrowing, not a lie about a foreign row. A double assertion is still an assertion. Core already rejects the double-assertion form on its own; this rule rejects each `as` in the domain.

source.work: pstack principles (boundary, domain, reader load, idempotency, legacy deletion, proof)
source.paraphrase: Stateful changes belong to named operations. A bag of optional fields repeats a shape assumption instead of encoding the change the domain allows.

invariants.why: A Partial patch hides which fields the operation is allowed to change. Callers invent combinations the domain never named.
invariants.fixHint: Replace the patch with a named operation whose parameters are the fields it actually changes.
invariants.avoid: A type alias `type Patch = Partial<Order>` is not a parameter, so this rule does not see it. Intersecting Partial with `{ id: string }` does not name the operation.

source.work: pstack principles (boundary, domain, reader load, idempotency, legacy deletion, proof)
source.locator: migrate callers then delete legacy APIs
source.paraphrase: When a new internal API replaces an old one, move the callers and delete the old API in the same wave instead of leaving a compatibility layer behind.

invariants.why: A compatibility path keeps two APIs alive. Callers of the old one never move, so the deletion the change was for does not happen.
invariants.fixHint: Point the caller at the new module and delete the legacy file in the same change.
invariants.avoid: Only module specifiers count (import/export sources, TS `import x = require()`, and the first argument of `import()` and `require()`), and only project-internal ones starting with `./`, `../`, `@/`, `~/` or `#`. A template literal counts when its text starts with one of those prefixes, even if a `${…}` comes before the legacy segment. Plain strings such as i18n namespaces (`estimateTemplates.legacy`) and bare package subpaths such as `pdfjs-dist/legacy/...` are not this rule. A name like legacy-adapter has no `.legacy` suffix and no `/legacy` segment, so it is not this rule either. Known holes: a specifier ending in `.legacy.ts` (the suffix is `.ts`, not end-of-string); custom tsconfig path aliases such as `@app/legacy/x`; bare specifiers resolved through `baseUrl` such as `src/legacy/x`; template literals that start with `${…}`; and resolver or mock calls that are not plain `require()`/`import()`, such as `require.resolve()`, `module.require()`, `(require)()`, `import.meta.resolve()`, `jest.mock()` and `vi.mock()`.
